TIMESHARE PURCHASE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Vacation Resort, Unit 204, Week 12

DECLARATION OF PURCHASER, TIME-SHARE PLAN, AND PURCHASE PRICE
This information sheet describes California statutory law under the Vacation Ownership and Time-Share Act of 2004 (Bus. & Prof. Code § 11210 et seq.) as it relates to a time-share purchase in which Jordan Alex Lee is named as purchaser, for the time-share plan described as: Acme Vacation Resort, Unit 204, Week 12, at a purchase price of $18,000. As described elsewhere in this information sheet, California law gives Jordan Alex Lee a statutory right to void this purchase contract, without penalty, within seven calendar days — or a longer period if the purchase contract itself provides one — after the later of (a) Jordan Alex Lee's receipt of the public report required for this time-share plan, or (b) the date this purchase contract is executed (Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(a)). This declaration states these facts about the transaction and about that statutory right; it does not itself constitute the notice of cancellation that the Act separately requires to appear, in conspicuous type, immediately before the purchaser's signature space in the actual purchase contract, and it does not calculate, extend, or waive any specific cancellation deadline for this purchase.

TWO STATUTORY CATEGORIES OF TIME-SHARE INTEREST: TIME-SHARE ESTATE AND TIME-SHARE USE
California's Vacation Ownership and Time-Share Act of 2004 (Bus. & Prof. Code § 11210 et seq., within the Business and Professions Code's Real Estate division) defines the terms it uses in Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212. A "time-share interest" is not one uniform kind of right — the statute defines it to mean either of two distinct things. A "time-share estate" is the right to occupy a time-share property coupled with a freehold estate, or an estate for years with a future interest, in the time-share property or a specified portion of it — an actual interest in real property. A "time-share use," by contrast, is the same right to occupy a time-share property, but a right that is not coupled with a freehold interest or with an estate for years with a future interest — a right to occupy without an accompanying real-property interest. The statute separately defines a "time-share plan" as the broader arrangement, scheme, or device — whether by membership agreement, sale, lease, deed, license, right-to-use agreement, or other means — under which a purchaser, in exchange for consideration, obtains ownership rights in, or the right to use, accommodations for a period of less than a full year during a given year, on a recurring basis for more than one year (not necessarily consecutive years). A time-share plan can be a "single site time-share plan" (rights at one property) or a "multisite time-share plan" (rights across more than one component site, as either a specific or a nonspecific interest); which category describes a particular offering determines which of the Act's registration and disclosure rules described elsewhere in this information sheet apply to it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Time-share interest” means and includes either of the following:(1) A “time-share estate,” which is the right to occupy a time-share property, coupled with a freehold estate or an estate for years with a future interest in a time-share property or a specified portion thereof.(2) A “time-share use,” which is the right to occupy a time-share property, which right is neither coupled with a freehold interest, nor coupled with an estate for years with a future interest, in a time-share property."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(x) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, definitions of "time-share estate" and "time-share use" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11212.)
  "“Time-share plan” means any arrangement, plan, scheme, or similar device, other than an exchange program, whether by membership agreement, sale, lease, deed, license, right to use agreement, or by any other means, whereby a purchaser, in exchange for consideration, receives ownership rights in or the right to use accommodations for a period of time less than a full year during any given year, on a recurring basis for more than one year, but not necessarily for consecutive years."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(z) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, definition of "time-share plan" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11212.)
  Known gap: This document is informational only: it does not itself determine which statutory category — time-share estate or time-share use, single-site or multisite — describes any specific timeshare interest or plan; that depends on the actual time-share instrument and disclosures for that offering, which this information sheet does not supply. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory categories California uses for a time-share interest — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific timeshare purchase, or that every state draws the same estate/use distinction; some states use different terminology (for example, describing all timeshares as a form of membership or club interest) or regulate timeshares primarily as securities rather than as real property or contract interests. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212 — treated as one source, not independent.

THE STATUTORY RIGHT TO CANCEL A TIME-SHARE PURCHASE CONTRACT WITHOUT PENALTY
California law gives a purchaser who has made an offer to purchase a time-share interest a specific statutory right to void the purchase contract. Under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(a), the purchase contract is voidable by the purchaser, without penalty, within seven calendar days — or a longer period if the contract itself provides one — after the later of (1) the purchaser's receipt of the public report for the time-share plan, or (2) the execution of the purchase contract. This same seven-calendar-day right, running from that same later-of trigger, also extends to an offer to purchase an incidental benefit, and to rights under an exchange program, when either is made on the same day as, or within seven calendar days after, a sales presentation for the time-share interest. The statute requires the purchase contract itself to state the seven-day cancellation period and the name and mailing address to which a cancellation notice must be delivered. A cancellation notice is deemed timely if given not later than midnight of the seventh calendar day measured from that later trigger date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) The purchase contract entered into by any person who has made an offer to purchase a time-share interest or interests, any incidental benefit, made on the same day or within seven calendar days after the person attended a sales presentation for a time-share interest, or any right under an exchange program, made on the same day or within seven calendar days after the person attended a sales presentation for a time-share interest, shall be voidable by the purchaser, without penalty, within seven calendar days, or a longer period as provided in the contract, after the receipt of the public report or the execution of the purchase contract, whichever is later."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, the seven-calendar-day time-share purchase rescission right and its trigger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11238.)
  "(1) The purchase contract for the time-share interest shall provide notice of the seven-day cancellation period, together with the name and mailing address to which any notice of cancellation shall be delivered."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, required in-contract statement of the cancellation period and notice address (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11238.)
  "(2) Notice of cancellation shall be deemed timely if given not later than midnight of the seventh calendar day."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, when a cancellation notice is deemed timely (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11238.)
  Known gap: This document is informational only: it does not itself void or rescind any specific purchase contract, and it does not calculate an actual cancellation deadline for any specific purchase — that deadline depends on the actual dates a specific purchaser received the public report and executed the contract, which this information sheet does not have. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's specific rescission-right structure for a time-share purchase — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific timeshare purchase; rescission periods, if any, and their triggering events vary by state, and some states measure a shorter or longer period running only from contract signing rather than from the later of signing or receipt of a disclosure document. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(a) — treated as one source, not independent.

REGISTRATION AND THE PUBLIC REPORT: WHAT MUST HAPPEN BEFORE A PURCHASER IS BOUND
Before a developer may sell, offer, or dispose of a time-share interest to a purchaser located in California (or offer an accommodation located in California), the developer generally must register the time-share plan with the Real Estate Commissioner, and Bus. & Prof. Code § 11226 provides that a developer, or its agents, shall not sell, offer, or dispose of a time-share interest in the state unless the necessary registration requirements have been provided and approved by the Commissioner, or the sale is otherwise permitted under the Act. As part of registration, the developer must prepare a public report — for issuance by the Commissioner — that fully and accurately discloses the facts about the developer and the time-share plan that the Act and its regulations require. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11234 requires the developer to provide that public report to each purchaser, in writing or, at the purchaser's discretion, in digital format, dated, and requires the purchaser to certify in writing that they received it. A statutory receipt form set out at Bus. & Prof. Code § 11236, which the developer must obtain from each purchaser, states that the commissioner's law and regulations require a prospective purchaser be given the opportunity to read the public report before executing a contract to purchase or lease a time-share interest, or before any money or other consideration toward the purchase is accepted.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(b) A developer, or any of its agents, shall not sell, offer, or dispose of a time-share interest in the state unless all necessary registration requirements are provided and approved by the commissioner, or the sale, offer, or disposition is otherwise permitted by this chapter, or while an order revoking or suspending a registration is in effect."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11226(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, prohibition on selling or offering a time-share interest without approved registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11226.)
  "The developer shall provide the public report to each purchaser of a time-share interest in a time-share plan at the time of purchase. The public report shall be in writing or in a digital format at the discretion of the purchaser and dated and shall require the purchaser to certify in writing the receipt thereof."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11234 (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, developer's duty to provide the public report and obtain a written receipt (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11234.)
  "The Law and Regulations of the commissioner require that you as a prospective purchaser or lessee be afforded an opportunity to read the public report for this time-share before you execute a contract to purchase or lease a time-share interest or before any money or other consideration toward purchase or lease of a time-share interest is accepted from you."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11236(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, statutory receipt form requiring an opportunity to read the public report before signing or paying (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11236.)
  Known gap: This document is informational only: it does not itself register any time-share plan, does not issue or supply any public report, and does not determine whether registration or a public report was in fact obtained for any specific time-share plan or purchase. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own pre-sale registration and public-report disclosure structure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific timeshare purchase; many states have a comparable public-report or registration scheme, but the specific agency, procedure, and required content vary by state, and some jurisdictions regulate timeshare sales primarily under general real-estate or securities law instead. The three citations below are drawn from three separate, independently enacted statutory sections (§§ 11226, 11234, and 11236), not subsections of a single section. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11225 — which its position early in this same article might suggest states the general public-report requirement — in fact does the opposite: it lists specific transactions exempt from the registration requirement (for example, an owner reselling a time-share interest the owner originally acquired for their own use); the general registration and public-report duty is instead stated in the separate §§ 11226 and 11234 cited here, a correction to that assumption. This document also does not independently verify the state real estate agency's historical name changes; it reports only that the Act's own definitions section, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(e) (quoted in a separate clause of this document), currently defines "Department" to mean the "Department of Real Estate."

THE CANCELLATION NOTICE MUST BE CONSPICUOUS AND PLACED IMMEDIATELY BEFORE THE PURCHASER'S SIGNATURE
California law does not leave the format of the required cancellation notice to a developer's discretion. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(d)(7) requires the developer to disclose, in conspicuous type, immediately prior to the space reserved in the purchase contract for the purchaser's signature, substantially a specific statutory notice of cancellation — set out in the statute itself — stating that the purchaser may cancel the contract without penalty or obligation within seven calendar days of receipt of the public report or after the date the contract is signed, whichever is later, explaining how to give notice of cancellation, and stating that any attempt to obtain a waiver of the cancellation right is void and of no effect. The Act separately defines what makes type "conspicuous" for this purpose: under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(h), conspicuous type means type in upper- and lower-case letters two point sizes larger than the nearest nonconspicuous type on the same page (excluding headings), and in any event at least 10-point type.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Conspicuous type” means either of the following:(1) Type in upper and lower case letters two point sizes larger than the nearest nonconspicuous type, exclusive of headings, on the page on which it appears but in at least 10-point type."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(h) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, definition of "conspicuous type" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11212.)
  "(7) Immediately prior to the space reserved in the contract for the signature of the purchaser, the developer shall disclose, in conspicuous type, substantially the following notice of cancellation:You may cancel this contract without any penalty or obligation within seven calendar days of receipt of the public report or after the date you sign this contract, whichever date is later. If you decide to cancel this contract, you must notify the developer in writing of your intent to cancel. Your notice of cancellation shall be effective upon the date sent and shall be sent to (name of developer) at (address of developer). Your notice of cancellation may also be sent by facsimile to (facsimile number of the developer) or by hand-delivery. Any attempt to obtain a waiver of your cancellation right is void and of no effect."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(d)(7) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, required placement and text of the in-contract cancellation notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11238.)
  Known gap: This document is informational only: it quotes the statutory notice language as the Act itself states it, but it does not draft or supply an actual, contract-specific cancellation notice for any particular time-share purchase contract, and it does not determine whether any specific contract's typography or placement in fact satisfies this requirement — that is a fact-specific determination this document does not make. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California imposes a specific placement and typography requirement for a time-share cancellation notice, rather than a general "clear and conspicuous" standard left to case-by-case interpretation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific purchase contract, or that every state imposes a comparable formatting rule. The two citations below are drawn from two separate, independently enacted statutory sections, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(h) and § 11238(d)(7), not subsections of a single section.

THE COURT REMEDY FOR A DEVELOPER THAT WRONGFULLY DENIES A RESCISSION
The Act provides a specific, if narrow, court remedy tied to the rescission right described elsewhere in this information sheet. Under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(e), if a purchaser seeks rescission under that section and a court finds that the developer denied the rescission in violation of that section, the court may also award reasonable attorneys' fees and costs to the prevailing purchaser. The statute frames this as a remedy a court may award once a purchaser has prevailed in litigation over a wrongfully denied rescission — a fee- and cost-shifting provision contingent on a court's ruling, not an automatically-triggered civil penalty, fine, or liquidated-damages amount that arises the moment a developer fails to honor a rescission request.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(e) If rescission is sought by the purchaser in accordance with this section, and a court finds the developer denied the rescission in violation of this section, the court may also award reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs to the prevailing purchaser."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, attorneys' fees and costs remedy for a wrongfully denied rescission (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11238.)
  Known gap: This document is informational only: it does not evaluate whether any specific denial of any specific rescission request would be found to violate Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238, and it does not itself constitute, transmit, or enforce a rescission notice. This is one state's statutory remedy, used as real evidence of what the Act itself provides for a wrongfully denied rescission — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific dispute, or that every state gives a time-share purchaser a comparable remedy; some states provide a specific statutory penalty or damages multiplier for this kind of violation, and some provide no remedy beyond ordinary contract law. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 11238(e)); no additional independent statutory source was found for this specific remedy. Business and Professions Code Division 4 (Real Estate) separately contains general real-estate-licensee discipline provisions (for example, grounds for suspending or revoking a real estate license) that could potentially also apply to conduct by a licensed developer or its agents; this document did not independently research or verify those general provisions, and does not assert that any specific licensing consequence attaches to a denied rescission beyond the fee-shifting remedy quoted here.

ONGOING ASSESSMENTS ARE A SEPARATE, RECURRING OBLIGATION CONTROLLED BY THE PLAN'S OWN GOVERNING DOCUMENTS
A time-share purchase is not limited to the one-time purchase price. The Act defines an "assessment," under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(d), as the share of funds required for the payment of common expenses that is assessed from time to time against each purchaser by the plan's managing entity — a recurring obligation distinct from the price paid to acquire the time-share interest itself. The Act requires this recurring obligation to be disclosed before a purchaser is bound: under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(d)(3), the purchase contract must state the initial purchase price and any additional recurring or nonrecurring charges the purchaser will be required to pay in connection with the purchase — including, but not limited to, the current year's annual assessment for common expenses and any financing charges — or, if the amount cannot then be determined, a good-faith estimate. Beyond requiring that current-year figure to be disclosed at the time of purchase, no provision of the Act located for this document sets, caps, or guarantees any future assessment amount, increase, or formula; the amount and any future increases are matters governed by the time-share plan's own governing instrument and budget, administered by its managing entity or association, not by a fixed statutory rate or ceiling.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Assessment” means the share of funds required for the payment of common expenses that is assessed from time to time against each purchaser by the managing entity."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, definition of "assessment" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11212.)
  "(3) The initial purchase price and any additional recurring or nonrecurring charges, or a good faith estimate if the amount of those charges cannot then be determined, that the purchaser will be required to pay in connection with the purchase of the time-share interest, including, but not limited to, the current year’s annual assessment for common expenses and financing charges."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(d)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, required contract disclosure of the current year's assessment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=11238.)
  Known gap: This document is informational only: it does not state, calculate, or guarantee the assessment amount for any specific time-share plan, and it does not itself supply or describe that plan's governing instrument or budget. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California requires disclosure of the current year's assessment amount before a purchaser is bound, while leaving the amount itself statutorily unfixed — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific timeshare, or that every state imposes even this disclosure duty. The two citations below are drawn from two separate, independently enacted statutory sections, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(d) and § 11238(d)(3), not subsections of a single section. This document did not locate, and does not assert the existence of, any provision of the Act capping future assessment increases or otherwise substantively regulating the amount of ongoing assessments beyond the point-of-sale disclosure duty described here; whether such limits exist for a specific time-share plan depends on that plan's own time-share instrument and governing documents, which this document does not have and does not describe.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF REVIEW
This information sheet, describing California statutory law applicable to the time-share purchase described above involving Jordan Alex Lee, has been reviewed by the parties named below. This acknowledgment confirms only that this information sheet was reviewed. It is not the public report described in Bus. & Prof. Code § 11234, it does not satisfy the written receipt certification that statute requires of a purchaser, and it is not the in-contract notice of cancellation, in conspicuous type immediately before the signature line, that Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(d)(7) separately requires of the actual purchase contract; none of those statutory documents or requirements is satisfied by this signature block, and each must be completed separately if California law requires it for this transaction.

expectedJSON.body: California law does not leave the format of the required cancellation notice to a developer's discretion. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(d)(7) requires the developer to disclose, in conspicuous type, immediately prior to the space reserved in the purchase contract for the purchaser's signature, substantially a specific statutory notice of cancellation — set out in the statute itself — stating that the purchaser may cancel the contract without penalty or obligation within seven calendar days of receipt of the public report or after the date the contract is signed, whichever is later, explaining how to give notice of cancellation, and stating that any attempt to obtain a waiver of the cancellation right is void and of no effect. The Act separately defines what makes type "conspicuous" for this purpose: under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(h), conspicuous type means type in upper- and lower-case letters two point sizes larger than the nearest nonconspicuous type on the same page (excluding headings), and in any event at least 10-point type.

expectedJSON.body: The Act provides a specific, if narrow, court remedy tied to the rescission right described elsewhere in this information sheet. Under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(e), if a purchaser seeks rescission under that section and a court finds that the developer denied the rescission in violation of that section, the court may also award reasonable attorneys' fees and costs to the prevailing purchaser. The statute frames this as a remedy a court may award once a purchaser has prevailed in litigation over a wrongfully denied rescission — a fee- and cost-shifting provision contingent on a court's ruling, not an automatically-triggered civil penalty, fine, or liquidated-damages amount that arises the moment a developer fails to honor a rescission request.

expectedJSON.body: A time-share purchase is not limited to the one-time purchase price. The Act defines an "assessment," under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(d), as the share of funds required for the payment of common expenses that is assessed from time to time against each purchaser by the plan's managing entity — a recurring obligation distinct from the price paid to acquire the time-share interest itself. The Act requires this recurring obligation to be disclosed before a purchaser is bound: under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(d)(3), the purchase contract must state the initial purchase price and any additional recurring or nonrecurring charges the purchaser will be required to pay in connection with the purchase — including, but not limited to, the current year's annual assessment for common expenses and any financing charges — or, if the amount cannot then be determined, a good-faith estimate. Beyond requiring that current-year figure to be disclosed at the time of purchase, no provision of the Act located for this document sets, caps, or guarantees any future assessment amount, increase, or formula; the amount and any future increases are matters governed by the time-share plan's own governing instrument and budget, administered by its managing entity or association, not by a fixed statutory rate or ceiling.
